newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CBANK MOVE SHOULD BENEFIT CAP MKTS - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CBANK MOVE SHOULD BENEFIT CAP MKTS - ANALYSTS.

text.p: The Czech central bank's move to lower minumum reserve requirements fell short of an expected rate cut, but analysts said on Friday the move still should have positive effects across the capital markets.

Late Thursday, the Czech National Bank (CNB) announced that it was lowering minimum reserve requirements to 9.5 percent from 11.5 percent, effective May 8. But the central bank did not announce an expected change in interest rates.
Analysts said bond and money markets posted early gains on Friday, with some predicting the move could add as much as 20 billion crowns in additional liquidity to the country.

"(This) will be placed primarily in the money and bond markets. Short-term yields have already begun to decline and the long-end of the market shuold follow," said Jack Schrantz, of Raiffeisen Capital and Investment in Prague.
Added Matt Starr of Creditanstalt: "There's an arbitrage opportunity developing between taking fixed income items in the Czech Republic and swapping them out into hard currency."
The Czech equity market, slow to react to most market news, edged up at the Prague Stock Exchange's daily price fixing, with banking shares leading the way.
"The news of a lowering of the reserve requirement could spark a rally in banking stocks, which would be a good time to take profits," said Schrantz.

Radek Vavra, head of Citicorp Securities in Prague, said he too expected banking stocks to rise, though the effects may be delayed. "If there's going to be an impact, it'll be long-term -- six months down the road."

The Czech economy has enjoyed several years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and the population, which has seen its wages rise sharply over the past few years, slaked its thirst for consumer goods.

However, some cracks have begun to appear with industrial output failing to keep pace with wages, and even contracting recently. Some economists say that indicates investment has not been effective and industry has not carried out restructuring.

Senior government officials have been vocal in blaming the central bank's highly restrictive monetary policy for the economic slowdown and many foreign exchange dealers are still convinced that the CNB will cut rates soon.
The crown held steady most of the day after an early dip against its dollar/mark basket.
On Friday the CNB fixed the crown at 29.790 to the dollar and at 17.315 to the mark implying a deviation from the midpoint of the crown's mark/dollar basket of +0.80 percent.
Crown rates on the interbank market throughout the morning and in early afternoon trading hovered around the same level.

Dealers said that while there was no rate cut on Thursday, they could not rule out the possibility that the central bank would move next week in tandem with the government which will announce a series of measures to spur the economy on April 16.
"The market is building in a possible interest rate cut, which could come...as part of measures the government is preparing to help the trade deficit," said one London trader.
"Investors have pretty well covered their positions now, but the market will remain volatile until the measures are announced on the 16th," he added.
